Manager's note — one-to-one with Gurpreet, logistics analytics team. Written by Sudha.

Gurpreet asked for time with me on Monday. He came in with a printed page, which I appreciated.
He explained that his father has had two falls since March and his mother can't manage alone on some days. He didn't ask for sympathy; he asked for a trial.
His proposal: work from home on Tuesdays and Thursdays, the days his sister can't visit. On those days he'll be online from nine to six, attend all calls, and deliver the weekly route-cost report every Thursday by five, which is the part of his work that needs deep focus anyway. He suggested we review after a month.
I agreed on the spot. It was specific, measurable and fair to the team.
Follow-up, one month later: every report was on time. His father has had no unattended days. We've made it permanent.

qa.q: Which days did Gurpreet propose to work from home?
How might Gurpreet have felt walking in with the printed proposal?
qa.a: He was probably nervous about asking, but prepared and determined to protect both his job and his parents' care.

qa.q: What else could Gurpreet do if his father's needs increase?
qa.a: He could talk to his family about adding paid help or sharing more days, and come back to his manager with an updated proposal.

qa.q: How does the proposal look from Sudha's side?
qa.a: Sudha finds it specific, measurable and fair to the team, which makes it easy to agree and later make permanent.

grounding: It shows someone explaining a parent's care needs to the manager and proposing two home-working days with defined output, which is accepted and protects care and job.

Friday night

I did it. I talked to Kavitha about Amma.
For weeks I'd been sneaking out at four to check on her after her hip surgery, hoping nobody noticed. They noticed.
Last night I wrote it all down: Amma needs someone at home on Mondays and Wednesdays, when the nurse doesn't come. On those two days I'd work from home, be on every call, and hand in the client dashboards by six each Wednesday. The rest of the week I'm in office as usual.
This morning I asked Kavitha for ten minutes and just read it out. My voice shook at the start.
She listened, asked what happens if a client meeting needs me in person on a Monday, and I said I'd swap the day. She said, "This is clearer than most proposals I get. Let's try it for a month."
I sat in the car afterwards and just breathed.
— Karthik
